A mine that loses its pumping for four days loses the workings below the level, and there are galleries down there that were abandoned to flooding a lifetime ago and are still, on paper, somebody’s property.
Rock that will not yield to a pick is taken by fire-setting: a fire built against the face and fed for hours, then the rock quenched and cracked and barred out while it is still too hot to lean on. It works, and it is how the hardest ground has always been won, and it drinks fuel and fills the workings with smoke that has to clear before anyone goes back in. Every man in the district can tell you the smell of air that is safe and the smell of air that is not, and a fair number of them learned it too late.
The smelters run on the streams. The water is dead (orange, sour, and useless for anything that drinks) but a dead stream turns a wheel exactly as well as a living one, and the wheels drive the blast. Furnaces run day and night because a blast furnace that is allowed to cool must be broken out and rebuilt, so the glow over the Pinna valleys does not go out, in any weather, in any season, and has not in living memory. Travellers on the Termin road at night navigate by it.
The Gangs
Labour comes in three kinds and they work the same faces.
Hired men are skilled and paid properly: hewers, timbermen, furnace hands, the pump gangs. They can leave whenever they like. Most do not, because there is nowhere within four days’ walk that pays half as well for anything they know how to do, and because the district has a way of making a man’s whole life happen inside it: he is paid at the company office, he buys at the company store, and the difference between those two numbers is the reason he is still here at fifty.
Pressed men are here for debt. A debt in Nysis can be worked off at the Pinna, and the arithmetic of how fast is done by the company holding both the debt and the wage book. Some of them clear it. The ones who do not tend to stop mentioning it.
Sentenced men are here because a court sent them. Terms at the workings are the standard answer in Nysis to a wide range of offences, handed down at Freeport and in every town with a magistrate, and they are handed down freely because the mines always want bodies and everybody involved understands that they do. Nobody calls this a labour supply. It is called justice, it is legal, it is public, and the men who pronounce it sleep well. The Pinna is where Nysis puts the people it has decided not to think about any further, and it does so in daylight, in open court, with a clerk writing it down.
The three groups do not mix off shift and do not much mix on it. A hired man at Collima on his rest day will not be seen drinking with a gang. Everyone in this district can place everyone else within a sentence and a half.
Fuel, and the Thing Nobody Says
Two fuels come in and they are not interchangeable, which is the whole basis of the district’s economy and is set out in Pinna Mines. Coal west from Termin heats everything except the furnaces. Charcoal east from Collima does the smelting, because charcoal is nearly pure carbon and coal is not, and coal’s sulphur makes the iron red-short: sound cold, brittle the instant it is worked hot, and an armourer can tell within three blows.
The district could survive losing the coal. It could not survive losing the charcoal, and the charcoal comes off a forest that is receding a little further every year to supply it. Everyone concerned understands the arithmetic. Nobody has anything to put in its place, and nobody is looking very hard, because the man who solves it ends Collima and knows it.
What Is Down There
The Pinna has been mined for longer than Nysis has existed. The Unmade worked this range, and worked it in ways nobody now can read: square-section galleries cut through rock that should have taken a season and did not, level floors, drainage that still functions, and voids sealed and dry where two hundred years of water has gone around rather than in.
Small claims break into these more often than is reported, and they are not reported, because a claim that reports one loses it to the Empire Mine, to the Conclave, or to whichever of them gets a man there first. So the old workings are entered privately, by four men and a rope, and what comes out of them enters the district’s economy without a docket and without a story attached.
Features

Slag in terraces, cooling, and the heat coming off it days later
Furnace glow over the valleys, in every weather, never out
Water the colour of rust, turning wheels perfectly well
Ore wagons on braked runners coming down the grades
Horse gins turning on the surface all day, lifting water
Fire-set faces, and the wait for the smoke to clear
Hired, pressed and sentenced men on the same face, not mixing
Company store prices, and the arithmetic that keeps a man at fifty
Charcoal in from the east, coal in from the west, food in from everywhere
Adits and shafts, worked and abandoned, unmarked and unfenced
Square-section galleries that nobody in this century cut
Old workings that go further in than anyone will admit

Quest Starter

A seam in one of the small claims has broken through into a working nobody put there: cut stone, square section, dry, and going down. The cooperative that found it has not reported it, because reporting it means the Empire Mine or the Conclave takes it. They have four men and a rope and they want someone who has done this before. They have also, in the fortnight since they broke through, become extremely careful about who they drink with.

atlas/piscis.title: Piscis
atlas/piscis.content:
A mile of drying racks, gull-clouds thick enough to throw a shadow, and the wall on the sea side only. 
Piscis
City · Nysis · Settled · Salt fish, salt, coastal freight · pop. ~2,400
Type: City · Condition: Modest · Disposition: Wary
First look: Protected by stout walls · Projects: Hunting or fishing · Touchstones: Independence from authority
Region: Piscis · Location: Coast
Location detail: The north shore where Falter Sound widens into the Sea of Bees
Exports: Salt fish above all, split and salted and smoked and barrelled in brine, in quantities that feed abstinence days across three countries. Coarse salt off the pans north of the strand. Fish oil, glue, and meal. All of it goes out by sea.
Imports: Everything else, and all of it by ship: grain, timber, iron, cloth, cordage, canvas, wine. Freeport is four days down the Sound and is, in every practical sense, where Piscis buys its life. Much of it is landed at Ostrea first, where the water is deep enough, and carted sixty miles up the coast road.
Piscis stands on the northern shore where Falter Sound widens into the Sea of Bees, built on a shelf of grey rock above a harbour that was never deep enough. Deep-draft traders anchor out in the roads and wait (sometimes days, in a blow) while lighters work back and forth beneath them. Everything that enters or leaves Piscis is handled twice. The city has made a trade of that inconvenience: there are more porters here than fishermen, and the lighter crews hold a charter, a hall, and a long memory for grudges.
The fleet goes out before dawn, long open boats under tan sails, running for the banks where the cold water turns. What comes back is gutted, salted, smoked or brined inside the hour, because summer here is unforgiving and the drying racks along the Nether Strand run for the better part of a mile. The whole city smells of it. Visitors stop noticing on the second day. Elsewhere in Nysis they say you can tell a man of Piscis in the dark.
The fish goes where the fasts are. A third of the year is abstinence, nothing warm-blooded may be eaten, and salt fish is what most of the region actually puts on the table on those days: cheap, keeps, travels inland, and permitted. Permitted if only just: the bloodless rank above fish in the Ecclesia’s grading, and Piscis has spent two centuries being told so by Ostrea, which sends oysters and a certain tone along with them. The two cities need each other completely and have never much liked each other. Ostrea has the deep water and no hinterland; Piscis has the roads and a harbour it must lighter everything into; the sixty miles of coast road between them is the only overland link either has that does not touch the blight, and both of them would be poorer without it and would rather not say so.
What shapes Piscis is that it is not, in any useful sense, connected to its own country. Between the northern shore and the rest of Nysis lies Ravenna, and the road that skirts it runs the blight’s edge for eleven miles before it turns inland. The road exists. It is on maps. Almost nothing goes down it, because almost nothing is worth what the passage costs: a cargo has to be small, dense and enormously valuable before it is cheaper to armour a convoy and walk it past the blight than to put it on a ship and sail four days to Freeport. Such convoys happen perhaps twice a year and are remembered by name. Everything else goes by water.
So the northern shore is a pocket. Piscis and Ostrea have each other, sixty miles of coast road between them, and Freeport four days down the Sound. Everything else is a decision about whether a cargo is worth the blight road, and twice a year something is.
The Wild Ground
The country between the northern shore and the blight is not empty, and it is not anybody’s.
The Verdani are the ones you can reason with. They come out of the green country west and north, they are purposeful, and they are not interested in a fish town: what they want is at Ravenna, where the extraction is eating ground they consider theirs. A Verdani party crossing near Piscis is usually going somewhere else. Usually.
The Broken are what the blight makes of people over time. Work gangs that walked off, camps that were never recovered, families three generations out there now who have never seen a wall. Drift taken past the point where it stops being a change in how a man thinks and becomes what he is. They are not a tribe and have no purpose beyond the immediate; they come in when the season is bad, take what is portable, and go. The Watch does not pursue them far, because pursuit means going into the ground that made them.
Everyone on this shore keeps a watch and everyone knows the bell. Raids are not a season and not a war. They are a fact of the place, like the weather off the Sound, and the shutters are built for both.
The Banks
And the trouble that actually costs Piscis money does not come from the land at all.
The banks where the cold water turns are the reason there is a city here, and Piscis is not the only fleet working them. The merrow are out there (grey, scaled, long-limbed, hunched, with eyes like wet glass) and they fish the same ground with nets of their own, and have done so for longer than anybody has been keeping a record. They are not beasts and they are not raiders in any sense a Freeport magistrate would recognise. They are a people with a fishery, and it is the same fishery.
For most of two centuries this was survivable, because the banks were richer than either side could exhaust. That has stopped being true. The Ecclesia’s calendar puts a third of the year on abstinence across three countries and Piscis is what feeds it, and the fleet has gone out further and stayed longer and taken more every decade to meet a demand set in a city four days away by people who have never seen a boat come in. The merrow have responded the way anyone would.
What that looks like from a deck is a net cut in deep water, a line fouled, and (three or four times in a bad year) a boat that does not come back and is found later with nothing wrong that anyone can point to. What it looks like to the merrow is not recorded, because nothing either side says is intelligible to the other; the merrow speak in clicks, grunts and whistles, and two hundred years of proximity have produced no interpreter, no treaty, and no meeting. This is a war over fish being fought by parties who have never once managed to say so.
Piscis is walled on the sea side and not on the land side, which every visitor notices and every visitor gets wrong. It is not for storm surge. Nineteen years ago the merrow came over it, and the town’s answer since has been to keep the wall in repair, keep a watch on the water at night, and not discuss the matter with outsiders.
And underneath all of it is a question the Ecclesia has spent a great deal of energy not answering. If the merrow are beasts, then killing them is nothing, and Piscis has been doing nothing wrong for two centuries. If they are people, then a good portion of this coast’s fishing fleet is guilty of murder over a disputed net. The Ecclesia grades every living thing that goes on a plate and has never once graded these. Both the fleet and the church prefer the silence, for different reasons, and neither has ever been pressed on it by anybody with the standing to press.
The urbestro’s customs house is not corrupt so much as tired. A captain who has worn out his welcome at Freeport’s Dock Walk can generally find a berth here and a clerk who will write down what he is told, which is why known associates in Piscis is a line that appears in Freeport’s own book of ship’s listings, in the column where a night clerk decides how hard to look at a cargo. Nobody in Piscis has ever asked to have it removed. And the urbestro himself draws, like every Nyssian mayor, a share of the Conclave’s annual rent for Ravenna: an income that arrives by ship from a chevayo he attends once a year at enormous inconvenience, paid for a blight that has done nothing for Piscis except cut it off from everywhere.
Features

Deep-draft ships riding at anchor, waiting on lighters
A mile of drying racks, and the smell that comes off them
Tan sails standing out before first light
Gull-clouds thick enough to throw a shadow
Gutting sluices running open down the rock to the water
Salt-cutters working the pans north of the strand
Lighter crews who settle their own disputes
A wall on the sea side of the city and none at all on the land side
Merrow nets in deep water, and the fleet’s own cut lines
Customs clerks who ask the second question but not the third
The coast road north to Ostrea, and wagons on it in all weather
The haze over Ravenna behind everything, on a clear day
The raid bell, and everyone knowing what it means

Second Quest Starter

A skiff has come in off the banks with a merrow in it, alive, tangled in a Piscis net and hauled aboard by a crew who could not think what else to do and are now extremely frightened of what they have. It is injured, it is not fighting, and it has been making the same short sequence of sounds since dawn. The urbestro wants it dead and the matter closed before the Ecclesia’s factor hears of it. Two of the crew have refused. Nobody in this city has ever had to decide what this is, and now somebody has about a day to.

Quest Starter

One of the twice-a-year convoys is coming up the blight road, armoured and late, carrying something the Conclave has not described. Piscis has been asked to send men out to meet it. Not escorted in, met, eleven miles down a road nobody walks. The urbestro has agreed before asking anyone. Whatever is on those carts, somebody out in the wild ground already knows about it.

atlas/polvokovrita-gap.title: Polvokovrita Gap
atlas/polvokovrita-gap.content:
A caravan crossing fast and not stopping, and the things half-buried in the dust that did not. 
Polvokovrita Gap
Remote · Mososi · The dust-covered gap; the direct south-western road
Region: Polvokovrita Gap · Location: Ravine
Location detail: A rift running forty miles south-west of Termin toward the Seka Lands
The name means dust-covered, and it is a description of the only route, not of the terrain around it. South-west of Termin the ground splits. A rift runs for some forty miles down toward the Seka Lands: walls of pale broken rock, in places a mile apart and in places close enough to throw a stone across, floored flat and level the whole way. The flat floor is what makes it a road. The reason the floor is flat is what makes it Remote.
It is filled with dust. Not soil, not sand: a fine pale grey particulate, ankle-deep in the open reaches and waist-deep in the hollows, that holds no moisture, packs under a boot and then releases, and hangs in the air for an hour after anything disturbs it. The Refiners’ Guild has looked at it and will tell you, without ceremony, that it is degraded Gray: programmable matter from something the Unmaking broke, ground down over two centuries into a medium that is no longer doing anything but has not stopped being what it is. It is not poison. It is not inert either. Long exposure produces the same drift the refinery hands know: a change in how a person thinks and feels and mends, arriving too slowly to notice from inside.
Caravans use it anyway, because the alternative is three weeks around. They go fast, they go veiled, they do not camp in the hollows, and they do not go at all when the wind is in the wrong quarter: a Gap wind can put a moving wall of the stuff down the rift at the speed of a horse. Everyone who works the Gap knows a story about it. The stories are consistent, which is unusual, and the consistent part is that the dust arrives before the sound.
What Lives In It
Nothing should. There is no water on the floor of the Gap and no possibility of any, and a surface animal that breathes forty miles of Gray particulate does not last a season. And yet the rift carries a complete food chain, three tiers deep, and the reason is that none of it lives on the floor. It lives in the walls, and it comes out.
A rift is a wound, and the rock either side of this one is broken to a great depth: fissures, undercuts, chimneys and collapsed voids running back into the country on both sides. Deep in that there is water: seeps, not springs, working slowly through the rock and never reaching daylight. Around the seeps is a lightless system of fungus, blind insects and the things that eat them, and it has been there far longer than the dust has.
Trogs work that system and are the foundation of everything above them. Warm-blooded burrowing reptiles, scaled, long-clawed, heavy through the tail, with a hide that carries a faint green-white luminescence, which is not decoration in a place with no light but the only illumination in the entire system. They tunnel constantly, they seal behind themselves, and the dust does not get into a trog run. They come to the surface at night and at the mouths, and that is where they stop being the top of anything.
Wyverns nest in the walls, high, in the undercuts and the chimney mouths, and hunt the rift floor the way a hawk hunts a hedgerow, except the hedgerow is forty miles long, a mile wide in places and flat, with nothing on it taller than a cart. It is the best hunting corridor in the region and they have it to themselves. These are the iron breed and they are the heaviest-plated wyverns anybody has recorded, with a hide that genuinely rings when it is struck, and the reason for that is in the next paragraph. They take trogs at the mouths, they take stray stock, and roughly once a year they take a person off the back of a moving caravan, which the caravan discovers at the next halt.
Wyrms are underneath. Massive, serpentine, wingless, short-legged and enormously long-lived, they lair in the deep voids, sleep for weeks at a stretch, and wake hungry. They have poor eyes by daylight standards and it does not matter: a wyrm hunts by vibration, and it can read the ground the way a person reads a page.
Which brings this whole ecology to a single point that everybody working the Gap has learned without ever being told the mechanism. Fine dust, forty miles of it, ankle-deep and level, is the finest medium for transmitting footfall that exists anywhere. A caravan crossing the Gap fast (which is the only sensible way to cross it) is a drum roll running the length of the rift floor, audible through the ground to something that is not listening with its ears. Going quickly is correct and it is also exactly what is being detected.
And the hollows. The reason nobody camps in the hollows is not the depth of the dust, or the bad air, or the difficulty of getting a cart out. It is that waist-deep dust will cover a wyrm completely, and does, and has. Nobody who works the route can tell you this in those words. What they can tell you is which hollows, and they are all agreed, and the list has not changed in thirty years.
The Dust Goes Up
There is one further thing and the Refiners’ Guild has written it down without publishing it. Degraded Gray in the ground does not stay in the ground. It goes into the seep water and into the fungus and into the blind things, and a trog that spends its life in that system carries more of it than the rock does; a wyvern that eats trogs for forty years carries more than the trogs; and a wyrm that eats both and lives for two centuries carries more than anything else in the region.
That is what the metallic sheen on a Gap wyvern actually is. Gray in the dermal layer, concentrated up three tiers of a food chain, doing what Gray does: binding to matter and making it structural. It is why the plating is heavier here than in the Tempest country, why a crossbow bolt skids off one, and why an old wyrm in the Gap is a genuinely difficult problem rather than merely a large animal.
It also means the caravan men and the animals are undergoing the same process by different routes. The men breathe it and get drift. The wyrms eat it and get armour. Nobody has ever remarked on the symmetry, because the two groups have never once had a conversation.
Features

Pale rock walls, a mile apart or close enough to touch
A floor flat and level for forty miles
Grey dust ankle-deep, waist-deep in the hollows
Air still hazy an hour after anything passes
Veiled caravans moving fast and not stopping
Hollows that nobody camps in, and the same list of them for thirty years
Wind putting a wall of dust down the rift with no warning
Things half-buried and preserved dry: carts, bones, gear
No water, and no possibility of any
Drift in anyone who works the route for a living
Green-white glow at a fissure mouth after dark
Wyvern nests high in the chimneys, and the whitewash below them
A bolt skidding off plating that rings when it is struck
Forty miles of level dust carrying every footfall to something

Second Quest Starter

A Refiners’ Guild man has worked out that the Gap is loading Gray into everything that lives in it, tier by tier, and wants to know how far up it has gone. He needs hide off a wyrm, and it has to come off a living one, because nobody has ever recovered a dead wyrm from the Gap: the dust covers a carcass inside a day and it is never found again. He has funding and a plan and has never set foot in the rift.
The caravan men have refused at any price and have been polite about why, and the reason is not the wyrm. If the dust concentrates in a trog and a wyvern and a wyrm, it concentrates in a man, and drift on this route stops being exposure and becomes something that adds up over a working life. Every one of them has already done the arithmetic in his head. None of them wants the number from a man who will go home afterwards.

Quest Starter

A caravan is overdue in the Gap and the wind has been wrong for four days. There is a window of perhaps a day and a half before it turns again. Whatever is standing out there in the dust has been standing there long enough that the question is no longer rescue, except that someone is paying as though it is.

atlas/profunda-forest.title: Profunda Forest
atlas/profunda-forest.content:
Clan sigils cut chest-high and kept fresh, a drop-stone on the margin, and eyes holding the firelight. 
Profunda Forest
Boundary · Nysis · Old-growth timber; the interior claimed
Region: Profunda Forest · Location: Forest
Location detail: The country on the southern flank of the Malperm, worked from Fluenti at its margin
The Profunda is the largest unbroken forest in the region and the only one whose middle nobody has seen. It fills the country between the Oray Hills and the northern flank of the Malperm Mtns, and its southern margin is worked hard: this is where Fluenti’s cut is, and the cut has been pushed further in every decade for a century. What that has produced is a graded forest: a fringe of stumps and regrowth, then twenty years of second growth, then the working face, and then, past the working face, the actual Profunda.
The old growth is a different order of thing. Trees five and six feet through, standing far enough apart that the floor is open and dim and covered in a deep springy litter that takes footprints and holds them for months. Very little undergrowth. Very little sound. The canopy is high enough that weather happens above it and arrives at ground level late and softened. River-drivers who have worked the upper reaches describe it in the flattened voice people use for things they have decided not to think about, and the standing advice at Fluenti is that you may go in and you may go out but you do not stop.
The interior is not empty and it is not unclaimed. It is claimed in writing, and the writing is on the trees.
The Varou
See also Varou.
They stand a head over a tall man and are built through the shoulder in a way that reads wrong at distance before you understand what you are looking at. Long faces, pointed ears, a snout rather than a nose. Grey and umber and black. Their hair is worn long and is groomed with enormous care: plaited, weighted, hung with beads and bone and worked metal and small trophies whose provenance is not explained, so that a varou in good order is the most ornamented person in the region, and looks it, and knows it. At night the eyes take a fire and hold it, yellow, and go on holding it after the rest of the shape has stopped being visible.
They are not from anywhere else. They are Nyssian: Touched, out of the same towns as everybody, in whom the wolf came up strongly and then kept coming up once families carrying it found one another. Five or six generations of that and it stopped being a chance of birth and became a people. Why they left is not a story anybody needs told: the Ecclesia grades a man by how little beast is in him, and the machinery that takes a marked child out of its parents’ house has been running for two hundred years.
What matters is what happened after they left, and it is this. A people driven off every piece of ground they ever stood on took a forest, and having taken it have never in a hundred and eighty years given back one foot of it, to anyone, for any reason. Territory is not one varou value among several. It is the organising fact of the whole society, and everything else (the clans, the feuds, the marks, the war with the Verdani) proceeds from it.
Territory
There is no varou nation and no council and nothing anybody could sign a treaty with. There are clans, each holding ground, each with a mark, and each perfectly willing to take a neighbour’s holding if the neighbour looks weak enough to lose it.
The marks are cut into trees along every boundary: a clan sigil, chest height, kept fresh, recut by somebody whose job that is. They are not decorative and they are not folklore. They are a legal instrument, addressed to other varou, and every varou in the Profunda can read every mark in it. That outsiders cannot is not the varou’s problem and has never been treated as one.
Ignoring a mark is understood to be a declaration. There are two places on the southern margin where Nysis built a settlement past a line it could not read, and both are ruins now, and both carry the sigil of the clan that ended them cut deep into the standing timber around the clearing. Fluenti knows where they are. Fluenti does not take parties out to look at them.
The clans fight each other constantly and have done for six generations: holdings shift, a clan is broken and absorbed, a mark stops being recut and something else appears over it. Outsiders who learn this tend to conclude the varou are weak, being divided. They are not divided about the forest. They are divided about which of them owns which part of it, which is a completely different argument, and the moment anyone comes in from outside it is set down and picked up again afterwards.
And they are at war with the Verdani. This is the piece nobody in Fluenti has any idea about. The Verdani want the Profunda (it is the largest living green in the region and there is real Verdant flow in the deep stands) and they have moved on it repeatedly across a century and a half, in the patient incremental way they do everything, and they have been driven out every time. The famous absence of Verdani sign in the interior is not a courtesy between neighbours. It is a war record. Mask Risen have been walked into this forest and have been taken apart, and a Verdani elder in Arbora can tell you what that cost and will not.
The Bloodcall
Running with the inheritance is a nervous quirk: an unusual sensitivity to ambient Crimson, and to the smell of fresh blood, which together produce a rising, narrowing, physically insistent state that is very hard to stop once it has started. Nobody transforms. It is closer to the first second of a real fight, sustained, amplified, and arriving without permission.
Holding it back is the central discipline of varou life and the thing children are raised into before anything else. A kill is bled and dressed far out by people whose particular business that is. A cut hand is taken outside before anybody looks at it. A stranger would take their manners around injury for extreme courtesy and be half right. They are the accumulated etiquette of a people for whom a domestic accident can end a household. They also do not go near blight, ever, since Crimson pools at a fringe, which is why the varou have no interest whatever in Ravenna and never will.
And in war they let it go on purpose.
That is the part outsiders do not survive learning. A varou raiding party comes at night, quiet, disciplined and entirely in command of itself, and at the moment of contact chooses to stop being any of those things. What crosses the last thirty yards is not a soldier. Afterwards there is a clan that has to sit with what its own people did, and a mark to recut, and an understanding on all sides about why the line was where it was.
What Fluenti Calls Trade
At three or four places along the margin there are drops: a flat stone, a split trunk, a stump nobody has cut. A Fluenti woodsman leaves salt, iron, needles, cloth, worked tools, and once a year a great deal of good rope. He comes back in four days and it is gone, and there are furs, or honey, or resin, or a length of deep-stand timber with no knot in forty feet.
Fluenti calls this trade and has called it that for a century, and it is not. It is a licence, renewed annually, on ground the varou consider theirs and are allowing to be cut. The cut has advanced a mile a decade because a mile a decade is what has been permitted, one silent negotiation at a time, by a counterparty Fluenti has never met and does not believe exists.
The whole conversation is conducted in what comes back, and there is a grammar to it that Fluenti follows exactly and has entirely forgotten the meaning of.
Goods taken, goods left. The ordinary case. The licence stands, the rate holds, the face may go on where it is going.
Goods taken, nothing left. This is the one that matters, and it is not a threat. It is a notice, and what it says is: you have taken and given nothing worth having, and there is no goodwill here this year. No warning follows it and none is coming. The correct answer is to stop where you are, work only ground already cut, and leave a heavier drop next season with nothing asked. Fluenti’s drop-men know to do this. They know it as bad luck rather than as diplomacy (a stone that eats) and they do it anyway, which has been sufficient.
Goods not taken at all. Rarer and worse, because it is ambiguous in a way nobody on the Fluenti side can resolve. It may mean the clan holding that margin has declined to deal at all. It may equally mean that clan no longer exists (broken and absorbed by a neighbour in some feud the loggers will never hear about) and that the ground now belongs to somebody who has never agreed to anything, has no interest in the arrangement, and does not know the stone is a stone. Untouched goods have preceded both of the ruined settlements.
Something left that was not traded for. A recut sigil laid on the drop itself rather than a tree. This has happened four times in living memory and on every occasion the working face came back half a mile within the month.
The men who work the drops have a folk explanation involving the forest itself and are not encouraged to develop it. Their fathers worked the same stones and taught them the rules as luck: never leave less than last year, never come back before the fourth day, and if it is still sitting there, do not touch it. Walk away and come again in the spring. Nobody has ever tried leaving less. It has held for a century, and the whole of Fluenti’s timber trade rests on a protocol nobody in Fluenti can read.
The northernmost drop came back empty this spring. The drop-man reported it, was heard, and was overruled, because this year’s stand is worth more than the trouble.
Why the Crews Come Out Short
Two causes, and the crews cannot tell them apart, which is exactly why the fear works.
Some of it is enforcement. A crew that cuts past a mark has made a declaration, in a language it did not know it was speaking, and the answer comes at night.
The rest is accident, and it is the worse of the two. A cutting crew is a moving hazard (axes, saws, wet ground, tired men) and sooner or later on any long job somebody opens his leg to the bone eight hundred yards upwind of a hold where a family is going about its afternoon. Nobody decides anything. It is fast and it is close, and afterwards there are people in the interior who have to live with it, and a crew on the margin who saw something in the dark and will not say what.
The varou understand both mechanisms perfectly. They have a remedy for the first, which is the marks, and none at all for the second, and explaining it would mean revealing themselves, and the day Nysis learns there is a nation of Ferals holding the Profunda, the Ecclesia comes, and it does not come to negotiate.
Features

Trees five and six feet through, standing far apart
Deep litter that takes a footprint and keeps it for months
Open, dim floor and almost no undergrowth
Weather arriving late and quiet through the canopy
The working face (stumps, skid trails, shouting) and silence beyond it
Clan sigils cut chest-high into boundary timber, and kept fresh
Two ruined settlements, and the mark of who ended them cut all round the clearing
No Verdani sign anywhere in the interior, and what that actually means
Yellow eyes holding a firelight after the shape has gone
Beads, bone and worked metal plaited into hair, and trophies not explained
Drop-stones on the margin, and a rate nobody has ever tried to lower
Rules kept as luck: never less, never before the fourth day, never touch what was left
Compass bearings that do not close, and no reason found for it

Quest Starter

A cutting crew has gone past the working face (deliberately, chasing a stand of timber worth more than the whole season) and sent back one man with a bearing and a request for help. The bearing does not reconcile with any map. Fluenti will pay well and will not send its own people. What Fluenti has not mentioned, because it does not think it signifies, is that the crew is working north of a drop-stone that came back empty in the spring, and that a company man was told about it in March and decided the timber was worth more than the trouble.

atlas/ravenna.title: Ravenna
atlas/ravenna.content:
The mill, the troughs and the drying fields, fenced off inside ground that is getting wrong by degrees. 
Ravenna
Remote · Nysis · Blight; Conclave mana extraction
Region: Ravenna · Location: Waste
Location detail: Inland between the shore and the northern Pinna, north of Collima
Ravenna is where the region’s mana comes from and it is the price the region pays for having any. The blight covers the country either side of the lower Duforq, between the Falter Sound shore and the northern Pinna, and it is not a place so much as a gradient: the ground gets worse, the vegetation gets stranger, the animals get larger and more deliberate, and at some point along that gradient you are in it. There is no line and no gate. The road runs through and the road is the only ordinary thing on it.
The Conclave holds the extraction monopoly here by state grant and pays Nysis heavily for it every year, and the monopoly is administered from three numbered Mana Refinement Sites strung along the river. Site #3 is the deep site and the largest. Site #2 is active and fortified, and its watchtowers are the first built thing most travellers see. Site #1 sat at the Duforq bridge and processed westward-flowing mana before river transport, and it has been abandoned since 140 SU, the Year of the Black Rain, when a trough went hard-steam and worked down into a single-lined black well and the well let go. Fourteen died where they stood. Corrosive material fell for hundreds of yards. Ninety years of Verdant reclamation have grown over the foundations in bloodthorn and the residual Black is still there and nobody has proposed reopening it. Guild hands do not discuss Site One.
Between the sites is the working blight, and it is worked by people. Rakers, trough hands, brass-crown operators, sieve crews, the drying fields. Nothing of value leaves this place out of the ground: raw manite is inert, and it is the trough line that makes it worth carrying, which is the whole basis of the monopoly and the reason the fence runs where it does. And nothing much leaves off the line either. Two locks on the vault held by two people, weights taken at four stages and reconciled by clerks who answer to Freeport rather than the site, a body search at the gate on every shift, and the Guild counting alongside because a foreman caught short-weighing is a foreman the Guild can remove. Men do get out with a thimble of amber in a boot heel once in a while and are caught more often than not. It is a trickle and it has always been a trickle. Everyone who stays gets drift eventually: the slow change in how a person thinks and feels and mends that long exposure produces and that arrives too gradually to notice from the inside. And the Verdani have been raiding the sites with increasing frequency and increasing seriousness, because the extraction is eating ground they consider theirs, and they have concluded that talking about it did not work.
The Guild
Ravenna is not survivable because the Conclave is careful. It is survivable because in 142 SU, after the sites killed enough people to make the deaths politically expensive, the order was made to accept the Freeport Refiner’s Guild, and the compact it signed, the Concordat of Labor and Light, is the single most important document in the blight. The Conclave conceded the Guild legal standing. The Guild conceded the Conclave operational authority inside the fence. Everything either party has done since has been an argument about where that line falls.
What the Guild actually does is keep a second set of books. It inspects every active site quarterly, it records conditions, casualties and incidents in its own hand, and it does not show those records to the order. It commissions its own training documents. It appoints an under-foreman at each site as a representative, whose job is to collect complaints and route them upward through the proper channel: dull, unglamorous, and the reason the process has teeth.
It works. It worked most recently on a senior foreman at Site #3 whose accident rate ran above Site #2’s and whose crews put in more overtime than anyone could account for, and who was quietly running an industrial-scale compulsion on his own workers. No individual complaint proved anything. Eighteen months of them, funnelled up by a Guild rep who never editorialised and never accused, crossed the Guild’s threshold for formal escalation, and a grievance was filed, and an inspector was assigned, and the man was recalled.
That is the system working exactly as designed. What happened next is not the Guild’s fault and is the reason this section belongs in the entry at all: the Conclave, presented with a monster its own institution had caught, chose to handle it privately. No charges, no public finding, no notice to anyone outside the order. A dismissal, a stripped crown beaten into slag in the yard at Site #3 in front of the whole crew, and a file annotated recovered to a peer institution. Nobody has ever gone to look at which institution.
The Crowns
The whole industry rests on perhaps two hundred people, and Ravenna holds most of them.
A waking trough does not run itself. Somebody has to stand at the console in a brass crown and speak the call into the slurry (wake, sort yourselves, come to the edge) and keep speaking it, and listen to what comes back, and know from the drift of the film and the sound of the paddle and the smell of the steam when a batch has Black in it and has started to feed on the red. Twelve troughs, four crowns to a shift, three shifts. Add the sieve hall’s construct and the lock-call rigs on the refining floor and Site #3 alone runs on dozens of trained minds, layered, each watching the others.
They are not made quickly. The Conclave spends the better part of twenty years on one, and the work eats them: an operator who has stood at a trough for a decade has drift, and drift is what ends the career rather than any decision. Most of a refinement crew does not see fifty. The order replaces them out of Freeport, at a rate that has never once been comfortable, and it has never troubled itself about the ones going the other way: the invalided, the failed, the passed-over, the quietly dismissed. They leave the fence and become Freeport’s problem and then nobody’s.
Across the Water
Forty miles east, across Falter Sound, there is a second blight of comparable extent and comparable richness, and it has never been worked. The Conclave has been trying to buy Spero for as long as there has been an empire there to ask, and Buralia has been refusing for exactly as long, politely, on a schedule. At Ravenna it is a standing joke: the good site, the one with no Verdani and no bloodthorn and no black wells, sitting there in the sun being nothing. Men who have spent nine years cutting a face they hate will say they can see it on a clear day, and cannot, and say it anyway.
There is a mission on that shore now. The order knows; a church buying ground in Buralia is not a secret and is not interesting. It is filed as what the Ecclesia says it is.
Two things follow from that, and neither has been noticed here yet. The first is that Ravenna is at the highest output in its history and is about to lose part of its market, because its largest buyer has spent a decade quietly arranging not to need it.
The second is that when mana starts appearing in Freeport at a third of Conclave rates, carrying Black, in volume (and it will), the order will not look across the water. It will look here, because this is the only place that mana has ever come from, and it will take the sites apart looking for the hole.
There is no hole. That is the interesting part. The controls at Ravenna are genuinely good and the accounting genuinely closes, and an investigation will spend a season proving it and come back with nothing, and be sent to do it again, because the alternative conclusion is that somebody else can refine mana and that is not a thing the order is able to think. It will be thought eventually, by somebody junior enough to say it out loud, and the moment it is thought there is exactly one place on the map it can point to. Ravenna’s honesty is what will crack Spero open. It is going to take years and cost the careers of several people who did nothing at all.
Features

Ground and growth getting wrong by degrees, with no line anywhere
Refinery works: the face, the mill, the troughs, the sieve hall, the drying fields
Site #2’s watchtowers standing over the road
Site #1 under ninety years of bloodthorn, fenced and unvisited
Uncontrolled outcroppings out past the fence, unworkable and left alone
Voids in the deep cut where the goo has flowed around something and not into it
Blight wolves, and worse, larger every year
Convoys of refined mana moving overland under escort, never by sea
Verdani sign at the perimeters, and what follows it
Workers with drift, and the flat humour they use about it
Guild inspectors quarterly, writing in a book the order may not read
Two locks, four weighings, and a body search at every gate
Brass crowns, and how few heads there are to wear them
The Buralian shore on the horizon, and the joke about it
Sites that will not open a gate to another site’s trouble
The Duforq bridge, old Conclave stonework, the end of it

Quest Starter

A quarry crew at Site #3 cut a bench deeper than protocol allows and put a bar through into a void: a dry, sealed, pre-Fall space the goo has been flowing around for two hundred years without getting into. Racked inside, in rows, are several hundred slender rods of Unmade manufacture, undamaged. A Guild rep spent an hour alone with one and established the thing that will get people killed: it lit. In his hands. He has no Veil, has never had one, and will never have one, and he held the rod and made light with it and then warmed his tea.
What he is holding is not a tool for making mages: no rod runs a waking trough, and everyone at Site #3 who matters knows it within a day. It is a household object. It is the thing every ordinary person in the world used to own, and there are several hundred of them in a hole in the blight, and nobody has reported it yet.
Every party that wants them wants a different world. The Conclave’s monopoly is not really on refining, it is on the claim that mana needs a licensed man: it will pay anything for the stock and then bury it in the deepest vault it has. The Ecclesia preaches a caste order built on who was born clean, and a device that puts working mana in the hands of a Touched laundry girl is not a threat to its revenue but to its cosmology; it would want them destroyed and would not want to explain why. The Brotherhood does not need to understand a thing to sell it. And the crew who cut the bench are eleven men on shift wages who have grasped roughly what they are standing on, have not yet grasped that there is no version of this where they keep it, and are three days from telling their wives.
None of the rods are charged. Nobody knows how they were meant to be.

Second Quest Starter

A convoy out of Site #3 has been taken. Not destroyed, taken, cleanly, by people who knew the schedule. The Conclave wants the cargo back and wants no one to learn it was ever missing. Recovering it means finding out who inside the site sold the timings, and the order has already decided what the answer will be.

atlas/sea-of-bees.title: Sea of Bees
atlas/sea-of-bees.content:
Sea of Bees
Remote · nobody’s · The open water; the only road out of the region · off-oracle
Region: Sea of Bees · Location: Sea
Location detail: The open sea north and east of the coast, from Piscis round past Ostrea to country nobody charts
North of where Falter Sound widens out there is no far shore. The Sea of Bees runs east and north past anything anyone in this region has business with, and what is on the other side of it is a matter of opinion held by people who have not been there. It is the one road out that nobody built, nobody owns, and nobody can close.
Piscis sits at the corner where the Sound opens into it. Ostrea is sixty miles up the coast on the last shelter it offers, and past Ostrea the shore turns north and stops being anybody’s. Between them the Nether Strand runs eleven miles of grey tidal flat, and that flat, and the banks off it, are what the two cities live on.
Why It Is Called That
Nobody knows, and the answer people give is probably wrong.
What they tell you is that in a settled easterly the shoal water off the Strand hums, low and steady, felt through a hull before it is heard, and that this is the sea working over the banks. That much is true and any Piscis boat can find it for you. That it is where the name comes from is a folk etymology of exactly the kind that survives because it is satisfying, and the name is older than any of the towns using it. What survived the Unmaking survived without its reasons attached, and this is one of the words that came through with the meaning stripped off it.
The Banks
The reason there is a fishing fleet is that the cold water turns here.
Somewhere off the Strand a cold current comes down and meets what is coming up, and where it turns it lifts everything from the bottom into the light, and the fish are there because the feed is there and has been for longer than anyone has been counting. The Piscis fleet works it before dawn in long open boats under tan sails. Ostrea works the flats and the leased ground inshore of it. Between them they feed a third of the region’s year, because the Ecclesia calendar puts a third of the year on abstinence and salt fish is what most of three countries actually eats on those days.
The banks were richer than either side could exhaust for most of two centuries. That has stopped being true, and the other side is the merrow, who have fished the same ground with nets of their own for longer than anybody has been keeping a record and who have responded to a fleet going further out and staying longer exactly the way anyone would. See Piscis for what that looks like from a deck.
The Deep Water
Beyond the banks the bottom drops and stays down, and this is where the region touches the rest of the world.
Deep-draft traders come in off it for Freeport, which is the only harbour on this coast that will take them without lightering, and Ostrea, which will take them and then leave them at the end of the road. Ostrea’s whalers go the other way: four to eight weeks out to the northern grounds, thirty men to a hull, out of a town with perhaps four hundred grown ones, so that when the ships are out a quarter of the city is out with them.
Weather arrives with about two days’ warning and no more, off water nobody is standing on. The insurance houses at Freeport write the Sea of Bees at a different rate from the Sound and always have.
This is Remote ground and it is worth being exact about why, because there is more traffic on it than on any road in the Atlas. The grade is a statement about support. A wagon that stops on the Termin road is a nuisance. A hull that stops out here is on its own, and everybody aboard knows the arithmetic before they cast off.
Features

No far shore in any direction that matters
The hum off the shoal water in a settled easterly, felt before it is heard
Cold water turning over the banks, and the gull-clouds that mark it
Tan sails standing out before first light, and the same boats back by noon
Deep-draft hulls riding at anchor off Piscis, waiting on lighters
Whalers gone eight weeks, and a quarter of Ostrea gone with them
Merrow nets in deep water, and cut lines coming up
Weather with two days’ warning and nowhere to put in
North of Ostrea, a coast that is on no chart anybody will sell you

Quest Starter

A deep-draft trader has come in to Ostrea off the northern water with a cargo nobody ordered, a crew who will not say which port they cleared, and a chart aboard showing eleven days of coastline north of anything the harbourmaster has ever seen drawn. The urbestro wants the chart. The Conclave has offered for the chart. The master says the chart is not for sale and that he is going back, and he is provisioning for four months.

atlas/seka-lands.title: Seka Lands
atlas/seka-lands.content:
A donkey train strung out a mile, a dry watercourse, and salt stacked white in the low south. 
Seka Lands
Boundary · Mososi · Dry grazing, salt, hides; clan law and no other kind
Region: Seka Lands · Location: Plain
Location detail: South-west of Lake Mater, beyond the Polvokovrita Gap, where the rain stops
South-west of Lake Mater the rain stops. Whatever the Polvokovrita Gap does to the weather coming off the water, the country beyond it gets almost none of it, and the Seka is the result: a wide, pale, open landscape of thorn scrub, wiry grass, dust, and dry watercourses that run three times a year and are the most dangerous thing in the region when they do. The horizon is very far away. There is nothing between you and it.
People live here and always have, and they are not enduring it. They are extremely good at it, and they have been for longer than Mososi has been a country.
The Cycle
The Seka clans work goats, sheep, and a small tough breed of cattle across ranges that would swallow a Nyssian county, and the thing outsiders never grasp is the timescale. This is not transhumance: up in summer, down in winter, home again. A clan’s circuit is measured in years: a named sequence of grounds, each grazed once and then left for three or four seasons to come back, walked in an order that has been fixed for generations and is adjusted only under duress. A child born on one ground may be twelve before the clan stands on it again and will have heard about it the whole time.
The herd is arranged the same way, by function rather than preference. Goats browse thorn and will find something to eat in a year that kills everything else; they are the clan’s insurance and nobody sentimentalises them. Sheep take the grass and carry the wool and hides that go out. The cattle are few, they drink more than they are worth, and they are kept anyway, because cattle are how a clan is counted: a herd is a ledger, a dowry, a history and an argument all at once, and a man who cannot recite four generations of a line of cows is not somebody whose word carries.
What people actually live on is milk, and curd, and dried curd that keeps for months and can be carried. Meat is a rare thing and mostly means something has died or something is being marked. Killing stock to eat is spending capital, and the Seka do not have any other kind: no granary, no cellar, nothing stored anywhere that does not walk. That is the strength of the system and it is also the whole of its fragility. A clan that loses its herd has not lost its income. It has stopped existing, and its people are absorbed by relatives within the year and their circuit is redistributed, and this happens perhaps twice in a generation and is spoken about in the flat tone people use for weather.
Water
Every law in the Seka is a water law and there are no others worth the name.
Digging is title. Whoever sank a well holds it, and their descendants hold it after them, and that holding does not lapse through disuse or distance: a clan that has not stood at a particular well in nine years still owns it, and everyone knows they do, and the mark cut into the rock beside it says whose it is in a script every Seka child can read. The marks are the whole register of property in this country. There is no other document anywhere.
Around that sits an etiquette that visitors find either beautiful or insane. A stranger’s animals must be watered (refusing is not done, and a clan that refused would find the story ahead of it for years), but watering is not permission to stay, and the distinction is exact and is not explained twice. Order of drawing is fixed: the holder’s stock, then guests, then whoever else is present, and a man who takes out of turn at a well in a dry year has done something his own people will settle before the injured party has to. Fouling a source is the one act with no procedure attached to it at all, because it has never been treated as a dispute.
And then there is the other water. The dry courses run three times a year, and they run from rain that fell somewhere else, often over hills a full day away, out of a sky that is clear where you are standing. What arrives is a wall of brown water in a channel that was dust an hour ago, and it takes tents, stock, and people who were doing nothing wrong. Every Seka knows the sound of one filling before they can see it, and the standing instruction given to children is not run but go up, and it is given before they can walk.
Salt
South, in the low country, the pans lie white and dead flat and are the Seka’s one export that the rest of Mososi genuinely needs.
The work is simple and brutal: the crust is scored and lifted in slabs, trimmed square, stacked to dry hard, and lashed in pairs onto donkeys for a train that goes out strung a mile long. Nobody owns the pans. The right to cut is held the same way a well is held, by mark and by memory, and the cutting seasons are staggered between clans by an arrangement nobody has ever written down and nobody has broken in living memory.
The pans yield a second thing that the clans regard as a by-product and price accordingly. The saltwort that grows on the sour ground around them is cut, dried and burned, and the grey ash raked out of the pit is sold by the sack to a buyer who comes twice a year and does not explain himself. It goes to Vitre, where it is half of what makes glass clear. The clans know it is worth more than they get. They have never been able to find out how much more, because the only people who could tell them are four days’ travel away and stateless.
What makes salt matter beyond the table is that out here it is money. A trimmed slab of a standard size is a known quantity (it does not spoil, it does not need an assayer, and it can be broken for change), and in the western reaches, where coin is thin and a Freeport gent means very little, prices are quoted in slabs and settled in slabs. The clans consider Materton’s merchants to be children at this. They are correct, and the merchants know it, and the exchange rate between salt and silver is negotiated fresh at every meeting by people who have been negotiating it their whole lives against people who do it twice a year.
What Mososi Gets
Mososi claims the Seka and does not administer it, and both sides find this ideal.
The Direktor’s writ is acknowledged in principle, ignored in practice, and invoked selectively by whichever clan is currently losing an argument, which is the only circumstance in which anybody out here has ever asked for an official. What the empire gets is salt, hides, wool, and a western march that costs nothing to hold because the people on it are not going anywhere and have no interest whatever in Mososi’s affairs. What it would cost to actually govern is more than the Seka has ever produced. Nobody in Typpe has proposed it in two generations.
The clans reckon a person by lineage and by herd, and the Puritan caste grading of the north (Pure, Prime, Second, Third) reads to them as a foreign obsession with facts that do not bear on anything. This is not tolerance and should not be mistaken for it. It is that they have looked at the question and found it uninteresting.
Features

Thorn scrub and wiry grass to a very distant horizon
Dry watercourses, and the sound of one filling before you see it
Dust that gets into food, water, eyes, and stays
Herds on a circuit of years, and grounds not stood on since childhood
Cattle counted, recited, and worth less than they cost
Salt pans in the low south, scored, lifted and stacked white
Donkey trains strung out for a mile
Clan marks cut into rock at every water source, and read by everyone
Wells, and the extremely serious etiquette around them
Prices quoted in slabs, and settled in them
Heat shimmer, and things in it that are not there
No imperial presence of any kind

Quest Starter

A well that four clans have shared for six generations has been fouled. Not dried, fouled, deliberately and with something that will not wash out. The dry season has eight weeks left. Every clan knows what the accusation will be, and every clan knows what follows the accusation.

atlas/spero.title: Spero
atlas/spero.content:
A mission wall far too long for the mission inside it. 
Spero
Remote · Buralia · Blight; worked off the books
Region: Spero · Location: Waste
Location detail: The eastern shore of Falter Sound, roughly opposite Ravenna
Spero lies on the eastern shore of Falter Sound, in dry country roughly opposite Ravenna: a blight of comparable extent and, by the two surveys ever made of it, comparable richness. Buralia named it Spero, hope, in the second reign, when a young empire that had just reached this coast expected it to pay for everything. Nothing came of that. There is no river to move product on, no road that reaches it overland, and no fresh water within twenty miles to run a refinery with, and for a hundred years the name has been a joke told with a particular face. That the two richest blights in the world face each other across forty miles of water, and that one of them made a Conclave and the other made nothing, is a fact Buralians raise more often than Nyssians enjoy.
Two hundred years of a blight left entirely alone is not the same thing as two hundred years of a blight under management, and the difference is the whole of Spero’s reputation. Ravenna’s outcroppings are surveyed, claimed, fenced and drawn down. Spero’s simply continued. The scrub country deep in has gone through changes with no parallel in the west; the surveys describe standing formations rather than outcroppings, both surveys use the word structure, and the second one, which was better funded and got further in, spends four pages being careful about what it does not mean by that. Nobody goes out that far now. There is no need to.
The Concession
The empire refused the Conclave (a Nyssian order arriving with a charter, a mine and a garrison) and has gone on refusing it, politely, every few years since the second reign, and the refusal is the one piece of this that is a matter of public record. What the empire did not refuse was a church. A dozen years ago the Pura Ecclesia asked leave to put a mission in the dry interior, for the souls out there, and offered a rent for the ground it would stand on. The empire took the rent and accepted the distinction, which is thin, and which suits both parties to go on treating as real.
Behind the mission wall is a refinery. Nobody is scavenging at Spero, and nobody anywhere is: raw manite out of the ground is inert and worth nothing, and turning it into something a caster can use takes plant, water, trained hands and a tolerance for what goes wrong. That is the whole basis of the monopoly and the reason two centuries of resentment never produced a rival.
The Ecclesia is not a rival. The Ecclesia is the customer: the Conclave’s largest buyer by a wide margin, paying monopoly rates on every seed burned in every rite, hospice, ward-lamp and reliquary it keeps, for two hundred years, to an order it regards as its own creature and its junior. It got tired of paying. It built the works with its own money, on its own ground, out of the reach of Nyssian law, and it staffed the works the same way.
What It Cost to Make It Work
Building it was not the hard part. Making it produce was. The Ecclesia had the walls up and the troughs in and could not get a usable batch out of them for years, because a refinery is not a machine you buy but a process somebody has to know, and everybody who knows it works for the Conclave.
So they took one. When the Conclave quietly dismissed a senior Ravenna foreman (no charges, no public finding, a file annotated and closed) the Ecclesia had the news within days, because it keeps sources inside Conclave administration for exactly this. He was approached twice, in plain dress, and accepted at the second meeting. He was gone from Freeport inside a fortnight. His Conclave file records him as recovered to a peer institution, and nobody has ever gone to look.
He inherited a half-finished operation and was given whatever he asked for. It still took five years to get Spero producing to a standard anyone would pay for, and it has taken five more to admit that the one remaining fault will not be fixed. He has not left the site in a decade and has not needed to.
Which is the thing worth understanding about Spero: in ten years it has not sold a grain. Plant, rent, wages, carriage, bodies: all of it outward, none of it back, for a decade, on the word of a foreman nobody outside the order has laid eyes on since. The stock sits in the magazine and grows. Somewhere in Freeport there is a ledger nobody wants read aloud, and the men who signed it have had ten years to become frightened of it.
The Workforce
The Ecclesia does not hire at Spero and could not if it wanted to. The nearest settlement is Alneta, down the coast, and it is four hundred fen-folk who want nothing to do with the place; beyond that there is nobody, and no road home. It does not buy locally either: the Buralians out west trade in captives constantly and would sell, but a taking in that country is understood to end, and the tribes count their people back. The church needs labour that nobody is going to count.
It has some. It made some.
The Pura Ecclesia has for two generations taken Touched children out of Freeport’s Stews as oblates: bought from destitute families with alms that are not called a price, given wholly and permanently, raised in the church’s houses and taught that they are unclean and that a lifetime of unpaid service is the only road open to them. They staff the laundries and kitchens and hospices of every Ecclesia establishment in the city, and Freeport considers the arrangement charitable.
An oblate who runs, steals, argues doctrine where the others can hear, or whose beast-nature comes up too far to be shown to visitors is not turned out: a turned-out oblate is an indoctrinated witness standing on a public street. They are told there is a house in the east where the work is harder and the cleansing is complete. They are walked a day east of Freeport to a small bay nobody watches, put onto a Buralian hull by skiff, and that is the last of them. The harbour chains and the Grand Office are never involved; the coast is not the harbour, and nobody counts boats on an empty beach.
The hull is not imperial and has no business being anywhere near this. It belongs to the Weirden Fen trade: one of the shallow-draft coasters that run fen produce into Freeport and come back loaded with what will not grow in standing water. Fruit by the barrel, medicinals for the hospices, fungus, smoked eel, and alder piling, which does not rot underwater and which Freeport buys by the shipload because Freeport is built on a sinking isthmus. Inbound they are full. Outbound they were never full, and a fen skipper who has spent his life counting a return leg in ballast does not need the proposition explained twice.
So the run east is backhaul. That is the whole reason it is invisible: nobody built a slaving route, they hung a deck cargo on a trade that has been going both ways for longer than anyone can remember. The boat is shallow enough to work an open beach off skiffs, which a deep-draft merchantman could not do and which is why the bay east of the city is usable at all.
The crews find nothing remarkable in it. Slaving is lawful where they come from and they take the cargo for chattel of the Nyssian orders: Conclave slaves, in their phrase, the difference between the two orders not being visible from that distance. But a taking in their country runs its term and the man walks home at the end of it; that is what the word means where they are from. It has not occurred to them to ask what the term is here, and nobody has told the passengers they are not going to a mission.
Casualties at the works run well above Ravenna’s, and there are no inspectors, no guild, no grievance procedure and no ceiling on a replacement request. And it does not run the direction people assume. Spero does not consume what Freeport happens to discard. Spero sets the discard rate. A house that used to send one troublesome oblate east in a year now sends six, because a request came down and nobody at that house has ever been told why. The almoners in the Stews have been instructed to be less particular at intake. The definition of unmanageable has moved, and it moved because a refinery four hundred miles east needed bodies, and not one person in the chain between the beach and the bay believes they are doing anything but the church’s work.
What the Empire Knows
Not nothing. An empire that maintains a post on the approach and collects a rent every year for twelve years is not blind, and the question is worth asking precisely because the answer is not yes or no.
At the capital, Spero is a line: a mission concession in a worthless district, granted to a foreign church, rent paid punctually and in silver. Nobody there has been told anything else, and nobody there has asked, because the district produces nothing and questions about it cost more than they return.
In the provincial administration, somebody knows better. The rent has been renegotiated upward twice, and the file gives no reason either time. The post on the approach turns people back, which happens to serve the mission perfectly, and no one has ever explained why an imperial garrison is providing security for a foreign religious house at imperial expense. It is understood locally that there is more behind that wall than a mission, and it is understood just as clearly that nobody is to write it in a report, because a report creates an obligation, and the obligation would be either to extort a foreign order (which invites the Conclave and Nysis into a question the empire has spent two centuries keeping them out of) or to shut down the largest source of hard silver in a district that has never produced any.
But what they think they are tolerating is mana. The empire refused the Conclave on sovereignty, not morality; a church quietly working the blight is a violation of the same principle at a scale small enough to price, and pricing it is what they have done.
What nobody in the imperial administration knows is the labour: that the works is staffed by Nyssian subjects imported by sea and worked to death inside imperial territory by a foreign institution. That is not a moral problem for anyone concerned; it is a sovereignty problem, and a far worse one than the mana. The moment it is spoken aloud the empire stops being the landlord who charged rent and becomes the accomplice who was paid, and it has handed Nysis a grievance it cannot answer and did not need to give. The Buralians have been taking money for twelve years to look at the front of a building. They have never once asked what came ashore on the other side of it.
One Crown
Everything Spero gets wrong comes from a single shortage, and it is not money.
A waking trough does not run itself. Somebody has to stand at the console in a brass crown and speak the call into the slurry (wake, sort yourselves, come to the edge) and go on speaking it, listening to what the trough answers, and know from the sound and the drift and the colour of the film when a batch has Black in it and is beginning to feed. At Ravenna there are twelve troughs and four crowned operators on every one of three shifts, and the sieve hall runs off a built amber construct the size of a wagon, and the refining floor has its own rigs speaking the lock-call into every cartridge. Dozens of trained minds, layered, watching each other.
Spero has one. It has always had one.
The order could buy the plant. It could copy the troughs, cast the crowns, and haul the water. What it could not buy was the twenty years the Conclave spends making somebody who can wear one, and it has never worked out how to get more of them. So there are crowns at Spero hanging on pegs with nobody to put them on, and the works runs at whatever fraction of itself one man can stand in front of. He cannot be at the troughs and the sieve hall at once. He cannot take three shifts. He cannot listen to twelve troughs, and he does not; he listens to two, and the others run to a schedule and are skimmed by men who were told what the film should look like.
That is where the Black gets in. Not through corruption or haste. Through the ordinary fact that nobody was listening. A trough left to a shift boss produces a batch that is mostly right, and mostly right compounds, and ten years of mostly right is a magazine full of product that no Conclave gate would pass. The output is also small. Far too small. Whatever the order thought it was buying, what it has is one man’s working day, repeated for a decade.
The order is aware of all of this, and has concluded that the site does not need more money, more plant or more bodies. It needs heads that can wear a crown, and there is exactly one place in the world they exist.
Buying three or four would get the troughs running. It would not fix anything, because in ten years those men will be old or drifted or dead and the order will be back where it started. What would fix it is one person able to train crowns at Spero, and that is a different thing to go looking for, and a much slower one, and it would not merely leak the Conclave’s monopoly. It would end it. Somebody is in Freeport now, taking as long as it takes.
The Shipment
Spero has sold nothing in ten years. What is in the magazine now is the whole of it, and it is going west in a single hull.
It does not go out on a beach or over a border. It goes down to the water, then south the length of Falter Sound past Alneta, and then in through the front of Freeport in daylight, because Freeport’s harbour is barred by chains slung between the Grand Pylons and there is no unofficial way past them. Entry is bureaucratic or it does not happen.
Which is where the Brotherhood earns its cut. The church cannot write a night clerk’s hand into the daily customs ledger at the Grand Office. The Brotherhood can. A ship stands off at the Fey Docks after midnight; its manifest goes up on the two o’clock runner; and somewhere between that runner and the morning the entry acquires a copper chit, a gate, an entry time, a flag code and an inspection grade of cursory that the ship’s captain has done nothing in his career to deserve. The chains come down before noon and the cargo lands as grain and dry goods, duty assessed and paid in full, which is the part that makes it work: nothing about the entry is irregular except that it is false.
The captains for this run are chosen for having nothing to lose. The last one was down in the Grand Office’s own book of listings as poor reputation, several prior infringements, and known associates in Piscis, which is to say the Brotherhood put a marked man on the most sensitive cargo the church has ever moved, and bought him a clean entry rather than a quiet one.
The forgery is not about duty. It is about the inspection. A full rummage at the gate would find the taint in an hour. So the entry is written cursory, the barrels go up the dock like grain, and the Brotherhood is paid and is not told what is in them.
The decision to send it anyway was not made at the works. After ten years and that much money, we will fix it in the next batch had stopped being an argument anyone senior was willing to sit through. So the whole decade goes west in one hull, on one forged entry, and every barrel in it carries the fault the site has never once been equipped to solve.
Features

Dry scrub giving way, further in, to something that is not scrub
Standing formations rather than outcroppings, and still growing
A mission wall far too long for the mission inside it
Refining plant modelled on Conclave designs, newer and cruder than Ravenna’s
Every barrel of water on the place hauled in from twenty miles
Contained tailings wells, and no inspector who has ever seen them
Brass crowns on pegs, more of them than there are heads to wear them
Troughs running to a schedule with nobody listening to them
Work gangs who speak Freeport dockside and were promised a mission
Children among them, and nobody at the works remarking on it
An imperial post on the approach that turns back everyone it is meant to
Imperial rent taken annually, for the ground and not for what stands on it
Two surveys, one of them careful about its own vocabulary
The name, and what people do with their faces when they say it

Quest Starter

A lay brother off the Spero mission has reached Freeport and stopped sleeping. He is not asking anyone to shut the works down; he has understood that nobody with the power to do it wants to hear about it. What he wants is for somebody who is not of the church to go out there, get inside the wall, look at the wagons coming up the track, and come back able to say what they saw. He can put you on a mission cart. He cannot get you off one.

atlas/suda-forest.title: Suda Forest
atlas/suda-forest.content:
Box cuts chipped fresh on every mature trunk, stills on this season's ground, tar running into a barrel. 
Suda Forest
Boundary · Nysis / Mososi · Pine, pitch, tar, turpentine; the crossing nobody admits to
Region: Suda Forest · Location: Woods
Location detail: South of the Pinna, on the sandy ridges where the hardwood gives out
South of the Pinna range, where the mountains break down into long sandy ridges, the hardwood gives out and the pine takes over. The Suda is a drier, brighter, poorer forest than the Nebula: open stands of tall red-barked pine on thin soil, floored in needle litter, hot in summer and loud with insects, with the ground showing white between the trees. You can see a long way in the Suda. Crews new to it walk spread out and stop posting a watch inside a week.
It is also the quietest ground in the region. A foot of needle litter takes every sound a boot makes and gives nothing back, and the insects cover what is left. The Nebula takes your eyes and leaves you your ears. The Suda does the opposite. Crews who have worked both will take the Nebula.
Naval Stores
The trade is resin, and everything downstream of it.
A mature pine is worked by cutting a box low in the trunk (a hollow that will hold a season’s flow) and then chipping a fresh streak above it every week or so, because a cut that is allowed to dry stops running. The gum comes down the face and collects, and a crew walking its ground does nothing all season but chip, empty, and carry. A good tree runs for years before it is worked out. A tree worked too hard dies standing and is left where it is.
The crude gum goes to the stills (squat clay and copper affairs set up wherever the season’s ground happens to be) and comes off as spirits of turpentine, with rosin left behind in the pot. Separately, and messier, resinous heartwood and stumpwood are stacked in a covered earth kiln and burned slow and starved of air for days, so that tar sweats out and runs down a clay channel into a barrel at the low end. Boil that tar down further and it becomes pitch.
All of it goes into ships. Pitch and tar for the seams and the standing rigging at Freeport and for every hull Ostrea sends after whales; turpentine for lamps, for paint, for medicine of varying honesty; rosin for a dozen trades. The Refiners’ Guild takes a quantity every year for purposes it does not put in writing. The barrels stack on the south road and go out by cart, and the crews are paid by the barrel and not by the day.
Fire
Every few years the Suda burns, sometimes for a month, and the crews watch the smoke and calculate.
They are not simply being callous.
